source: Original KaiSip study notes, organized by The IIA's CIA Part 1 syllabus effective 2025. KaiSip is an independent study aid, not affiliated with or endorsed by The IIA.
overview: Section B is about the person doing the audit: the five behaviors every internal auditor must show are integrity, objectivity, competency, due professional care and confidentiality. They sit in Domain II of the Global Internal Audit Standards and bind everyone in the internal audit function (the team that does internal audit work), up to its head, the chief audit executive. Inside each standard, requirements say 'must' and are mandatory, while considerations say 'should' (the preferred practice) or 'may' (an option). On a question, a 'should' action can still be the best answer because it is the preferred practice; what is wrong is an option that calls it mandatory, or one that treats a 'must' as optional.
analogy: Think of a football referee. The referee calls what they see, even against the home team with the crowd shouting (integrity). A referee whose cousin plays for one side tells the league and is swapped out (objectivity). They train every season and know the current rulebook (competency). They watch the risky parts of the pitch closely without claiming to see every foul (due professional care). What they hear in the dressing room stays there unless the rules require a report (confidentiality). A referee who fails any one of these loses the trust that makes the calls count.

topics.overview: Integrity is the base the other four ethics principles stand on. This topic covers telling the truth and speaking up under pressure, living up to the organization's ethical expectations, and staying inside the law and the profession's standards of behavior. It also shows where a concern goes once an internal auditor has seen it.
can_do: Choose the honest, complete response when a manager presses for a softer finding
Route an ethics concern or a legal violation to the party that policy and law name
Spot behavior the Standards treat as discreditable, such as an overstated credential
Explain why Domain II still binds an internal auditor who follows another ethics code

subtopics.name: Honesty and Professional Courage
subtopics.definition: Honesty and professional courage mean an internal auditor tells the truth, reports the full picture and acts on the facts, even when that is unwelcome or risky.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The board and management decide on what internal auditors tell them. A softened, inflated or missing finding misdirects their attention and destroys trust.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 1.1 Honesty and Professional Courage): be respectful, truthful, accurate, clear and open, including when you doubt or disagree.
Must not: make a false, misleading or deceptive statement, or hide or omit a finding or relevant information. Rate on the CAE's scale: overstating misleads too (14.3).
Must: disclose every material fact you know, in scope or not. Standard 1.1 names no recipient or deadline; KaiSip's reading: the decision at stake sets both.
Should (a consideration: preferred, not required): talk a hard case through with a supervisor.
Must, for the chief audit executive: keep a workplace where auditors feel supported in reporting evidence-based results, good or bad.
Must (Standard 15.2): raise a fix past its agreed date with the CAE, who judges whether the delay accepts risk above tolerance and, if so, escalates it (11.5).
subtopics.example: Lerato, an internal auditor at a bus operator in Durban, finds on an engagement (one audit assignment) that driver safety checks were skipped for months. The depot manager wants it worded as 'minor scheduling gaps'. Lerato stays polite, changes one loaded adjective the manager fairly objects to, and keeps the finding and its numbers as the evidence shows them.

review: Compare draft and final communications for findings dropped without a documented reason
Trace supervisor review notes to how each challenged finding was resolved
evidence: Version history of engagement communications with the reason for each change
Feedback from the management of reviewed activities on internal auditors' candor
audit_focus.recommend: Require a documented reason, approved by the engagement supervisor, whenever a finding is removed or reworded after discussion with management.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive approves the final communication; management decides how to respond

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: report what the evidence shows, in full, at its true weight and with respect; pressure, friendship or fear never justifies softening, inflating, delaying or dropping a finding.

exam_traps.trap: Dropping a minor-looking finding protects a good working relationship with the manager.
exam_traps.why: Leaving out a finding or other relevant information is forbidden. A respectful tone and fair wording protect the relationship; silence does not.

exam_traps.trap: Professional courage means confronting the manager and refusing to back down.
exam_traps.why: Courage is truthful communication and fitting action. The same standard demands respect, so the auditor listens and still reports the facts.

key_terms.definition: The head of the internal audit function, whatever the job title.
A 'must' in a standard: mandatory.
Communicating truthfully and acting properly in a dilemma or under pressure.

subtopics.name: Meeting the Organization's Ethical Expectations
subtopics.definition: The organization's ethical expectations are the conduct standards it sets, usually in a code of conduct and related policies, which internal auditors must know, meet and help uphold.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Internal auditors can only spot and report conduct that breaks the organization's expectations if they know them and the route a concern takes. The ethics framework route is in 1C3.3; possible fraud in 1D3.3.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 1.2 Organization's Ethical Expectations): internal auditors themselves understand, respect and meet the organization's legitimate, ethical expectations and help advance them.
Must: be able to recognize conduct against those expectations, and encourage an ethics-based culture.
Must: report such conduct as the applicable policies and procedures say, not by a private route.
Should: when a member of senior management is involved, the chief audit executive (CAE) reports it to the board; when the chair is involved, to the whole board.
Should: follow up on ethics matters involving the board or senior management and confirm that action was taken.
subtopics.example: Beatriz is CAE of a Lisbon hotel group. An internal auditor reports, as the methodology requires, that the chief financial officer pressed a supplier to hire a relative. Beatriz confirms the facts. Because senior management is involved, Beatriz takes the matter to the audit committee, which acts as the board, not to the executive team.

review: Compare reported ethics concerns with the route the ethics policy sets
Sample engagement plans for coverage of ethics-related risks and controls
evidence: Log of ethics concerns raised by internal auditors, with dates and recipients
Board minutes showing that concerns about senior management were received
audit_focus.recommend: Set a methodology for raising ethics concerns and agree it with the board and senior management.
audit_focus.decides: Management or the board decides the response to a reported concern

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: report conduct that breaks the organization's ethical expectations through the channel policy sets, whatever the engagement scope. Should: the CAE takes a senior management matter to the board.

exam_traps.trap: Going to the board is only a 'should', so reporting to senior management is just as good.
exam_traps.why: A 'should' is the Standards' preferred practice, so it is still the best answer here. It is not mandatory: only an option that calls it required would be wrong.

exam_traps.trap: Any family tie between a staff member and a winning supplier is a breach to report.
exam_traps.why: Standard 1.2 concerns conduct against the organization's expectations. A tie declared and handled as the code provides meets them; the auditor checks that the safeguard held.

key_terms.definition: A document stating the behavior an organization expects from its people.
Shared values and habits that make honest behavior the normal, expected choice.
The route that policy, law or the function's methodology sets for raising a concern.

subtopics.name: Legal and Professional Behavior
subtopics.definition: Legal and professional behavior means an internal auditor obeys the law, avoids conduct that would discredit the organization or the profession, and reports violations to those who can act.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An auditor who breaks a rule, or looks away when others do, cannot credibly assess anyone else.
how_it_works: Must not (Standard 1.3 Legal and Ethical Behavior): take part in anything illegal, discreditable to the organization or the profession, or that could harm the organization or its staff.
Must: know and follow the laws and regulations of the organization's industry and of every place it operates, and make any disclosures they require.
Must: report a violation you identify to people or bodies with authority to act, as laws, regulations and policies specify.

Discreditable acts include bullying, lying about a credential or showing an expired or inactive one, overlooking illegal activity the organization tolerates, unsupported conformance claims, and not accepting responsibility for mistakes.
Domain II replaced the profession's earlier separate ethics code. It binds every internal auditor, even one who also follows another code.
subtopics.example: Baraka, an internal auditor at a freight company in Dar es Salaam, learns that drivers' rest-hour logs are altered to hide breaches of transport law. Policy sends suspected legal violations to the general counsel, and the internal audit methodology routes them through the chief audit executive (CAE). Baraka reports the facts that day to the CAE, who takes them to the general counsel.

review: Compare each auditor's listed credentials with the certifying body's current records
Trace reported legal violations to the authority named in policy or law
evidence: Certification status confirmations obtained from the certifying body
Documented methodology for handling legal or regulatory violations
audit_focus.recommend: Document how internal audit staff report legal violations when the organization's policies are not specific enough.
audit_focus.decides: Management, the board or a regulator with authority decides the response

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: stay inside the law, make the disclosures it requires, and report a violation to whoever has authority to act, by the route law and policy set. Every part of this is a requirement.

exam_traps.trap: Management knows about the practice and accepts it, so there is nothing to report.
exam_traps.why: Overlooking illegal activity the organization tolerates is itself discreditable. The auditor still reports to a party with authority to act.

exam_traps.trap: Going straight to the press or a regulator is the safest first step.
exam_traps.why: Reports go to those with authority to act as laws, regulations and policies specify. An outside disclosure is made when the law requires one.

key_terms.definition: Conduct that harms trust in the internal auditor, the organization or the profession, such as lying about a credential.
The power to investigate, correct or sanction a violation.

topics.overview: Objectivity is each internal auditor's unbiased state of mind. This topic covers what objectivity is, how self-review bias, familiarity bias and conflicts of interest damage it, and how to judge whether a situation is an actual, potential or perceived impairment.
can_do: Tell an objectivity problem (the person) from an independence problem (the function) in a scenario
Judge how self-review or familiarity bias would weaken the results of a planned engagement
Decide whether a relationship, interest or past role is a conflict of interest, in fact or in appearance
Assess a former responsibility against the refrain rule, the 12-month presumption for assurance and the disclosure condition for advisory work

subtopics.name: Objectivity as a Personal Mindset
subtopics.definition: Objectivity is the unbiased state of mind that lets an internal auditor judge on the evidence alone, without giving way to personal interest or to other people's wishes.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Findings and conclusions are worth relying on only if bias did not shape them. Objectivity belongs to the person, so every auditor has to guard it on every engagement. Independence of the function is in 1A7; here we cover the individual auditor's objectivity.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 2.1 Individual Objectivity): keep an impartial, unbiased mindset in every part of the work, with judgments resting on a balanced view of the relevant circumstances.
Must: know your own possible biases and manage them. Bias is a normal human tendency, not bad character.
Objectivity means not handing your judgment over to anyone, including senior management or others in authority.
Independence is different: it is the function's freedom from conditions that would bias its work, and comes from reporting directly to the board.
An independently positioned function supports objectivity but cannot supply it. Each auditor still has to be unbiased.

rows.label: Belongs to
cells: Each internal auditor
The internal audit function

rows.label: What it is
cells: An unbiased state of mind
Freedom from conditions that would bias the function's work

rows.label: Comes from
cells: Awareness of bias, disclosure and protective steps
Direct reporting to the board and proper positioning

rows.label: A problem goes to
cells: The chief audit executive (CAE), or a supervisor that executive names
The board and senior management, from the CAE

rows.label: Where to read
cells: Principle 2 and Standards 2.1 to 2.3
Principle 7 and Standard 7.1 Organizational Independence

subtopics.example: An insurer in Jakarta has an internal audit function that reports straight to the audit committee. Reviewing the claims engagement, the supervisor finds that Dewi, the auditor, accepted thin evidence on six files because the claims team had been so helpful last year. The function was independent; Dewi's judgment had tilted. Dewi retests the six files against the criteria, and two findings are added.

review: Sample workpapers for conclusions that the documented evidence does not support
Compare signed objectivity attestations with the assignments made during the year
evidence: Supervisory review notes questioning one-sided judgments
Records of objectivity training, with participants listed
audit_focus.recommend: Train internal audit staff on common biases and add a bias question to the supervisory review checklist.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive decides how a disclosed bias is handled

subtopics.isaca_rule: Independence is the function's; objectivity is the person's. Must: every auditor keeps an unbiased mindset and manages their own biases. A sound reporting line never proves that an individual is unbiased.

exam_traps.trap: The function reports to the board, so its auditors are objective.
exam_traps.why: Board reporting gives the function independence. Objectivity is each auditor's own mindset and can be impaired on any engagement, however good the structure.

exam_traps.trap: An honest auditor has no biases to manage.
exam_traps.why: The Standards treat bias as a human tendency every auditor must be aware of and manage. Denying it removes the first protection.

key_terms.definition: A lean in judgment, often unnoticed, that pulls a conclusion away from what the evidence supports.
Letting another person's wishes or rank replace your own professional conclusion.
A signed statement; here, an auditor's declaration that they have no impairment or have disclosed it.

subtopics.memory_aid: Function is independent; person is objective.

subtopics.name: Self-Review Bias and Familiarity Bias
subtopics.definition: Self-review bias and familiarity bias are two threats to objectivity: one comes from judging your own earlier work, the other from leaning on past experience instead of fresh evidence.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Both make an internal auditor less critical without noticing. Errors get missed, professional skepticism fades, and the engagement's results become less reliable.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity): refrain from assessing a specific activity you were previously responsible for. This rule has no time limit.
For assurance, objectivity is presumed impaired if you held the responsibility within the previous 12 months.
Self-review bias also covers your own earlier audit work: judging a rating or conclusion you gave impairs objectivity, at least in appearance; disclose it (Standards 2.1 and 2.3).
May: informal contact with a unit builds trust but can wear at objectivity; rotating auditors into and out of assignments may balance the two (Standard 11.1, a consideration).

types.meaning: Losing a critical eye when assessing work one designed, decided or performed oneself.
Letting assumptions from past experience stand in for fresh evidence, which weakens professional skepticism.
Misreading information because of fixed ideas about a group of people, which leads to wrong judgments.

subtopics.example: Diego joined the internal audit function at a retailer in Montevideo eight months ago after running its accounts payable team. The plan now lists an assurance engagement on accounts payable, and Diego knows the process best. Diego was responsible for it within the past 12 months, so objectivity is presumed impaired. Diego tells the chief audit executive, who assigns other auditors.

review: Compare each auditor's prior roles with the assurance engagements assigned to them
Inspect planning files for the impairment question asked before staffing
evidence: Staffing records matched to auditors' employment history
Planning notes of the impairment discussion held before each engagement
audit_focus.recommend: Screen every assignment against the audit staff's former responsibilities before the team is confirmed.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive, or a delegate, decides engagement staffing

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: no assessing an activity you used to be responsible for; for assurance inside 12 months objectivity is presumed impaired, whatever your skill or intentions. Knowing the area best is the warning sign, not the qualification. Rotation is a 'may'.

exam_traps.trap: The auditor who used to run the process is the best person to audit it.
exam_traps.why: Deep knowledge comes with self-review bias. Inside 12 months objectivity is presumed impaired for assurance; the refrain rule never ends (see 1B2.4).

exam_traps.trap: Familiarity matters only when the auditor and the manager are personal friends.
exam_traps.why: Familiarity bias is about assumptions from past experience. A long run of clean audits can dull skepticism with no friendship at all.

key_terms.definition: Engagements where internal auditors test an activity against criteria and state a conclusion others can rely on.
An impairment the Standards assume without proof, such as assurance over a responsibility held in the past 12 months.
Moving auditors into and out of assignments in a unit or place over time.

subtopics.name: Conflicts of Interest
subtopics.definition: A conflict of interest is any competing personal or professional interest, tie or activity that could sway an internal auditor's judgment, or make it look swayed.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A conflict can damage confidence in the auditor, the function and the profession even when nothing improper happens, because others cannot see inside the auditor's mind.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity): stay clear of conflicts of interest and not let your own interests, or anyone else's, steer your work.
Influence can come from senior management, others in authority, the political climate or the auditor's surroundings.
Typical conflicts: interests that compete with the organization's, a chance of improper personal gain, self-protection from loss, and favoritism or nepotism (favoring relatives or friends).
A close personal relationship away from work, or a financial tie such as an investment, can be a conflict or look like one.
Should: the chief audit executive (CAE) guards against pay designs that reward bias, such as bonuses resting mainly on audited managers' ratings or on the number of findings raised.
subtopics.example: Aino, an internal auditor at a city council in Tampere, audited a road maintenance contract and found little. Aino's sibling manages operations at the contractor, and Aino, sure of being fair, had told nobody. A councillor learned of the tie and questioned the results. Nothing improper had happened, yet the CAE had to have another auditor repeat the work.

review: Compare auditors' declared interests and relationships with their assigned engagements
Evaluate whether auditor bonuses depend on ratings from the management under review
evidence: Conflict of interest declarations, with dates and the action taken
Remuneration plan showing how auditor performance is measured
audit_focus.recommend: Collect conflict declarations from the audit team before each engagement and drop pay measures tied to the management under review.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive determines the action on a declared conflict

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: avoid conflicts of interest. A conflict counts in fact or in appearance, so your own confidence does not settle it. Should: consider how others would see it. Relationships count as much as money.

exam_traps.trap: No money is involved, so there is no conflict of interest.
exam_traps.why: Family ties, friendships, favoritism and self-protection are conflicts too. The test is whether judgment could be, or appear to be, influenced.

exam_traps.trap: The auditor knows they will be fair, so nothing needs to be said.
exam_traps.why: Others may perceive an impairment even when none exists in fact. The requirement is to disclose it and let the CAE determine what happens.

key_terms.definition: Pressure or interest that pushes a judgment away from the evidence.
A situation that looks wrong to others, even if no improper act took place.
How an auditor is paid and rewarded; a poor design can reward biased results.

subtopics.name: Assessing Whether Objectivity Is Impaired
subtopics.definition: An impairment to objectivity is any situation, activity or relationship that may bend an internal auditor's judgments enough to change findings or conclusions.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The assessment decides what happens next. Calling a real impairment harmless taints the engagement; treating every past link as a bar wastes knowledge.
how_it_works: Must: recognize actual (real), potential (could arise) and perceived (as others see it) impairments, and avoid or mitigate them.
Must: refrain from assessing an activity you were once responsible for. The Standards put no end date on this.
Inside 12 months of holding it, objectivity is presumed impaired for assurance. After 12 months only that presumption stops: you still disclose, and the chief audit executive (CAE) decides.
Advisory work (advice, with no assurance) on a former responsibility: allowed, but you must first disclose the possible impairment to the requesting party.
Assurance where the function earlier advised: the CAE must confirm the advice did not impair objectivity and assign auditors so each one's objectivity is managed.

rows.label: Assurance over an activity you ran 8 months ago
cells: No
Objectivity is presumed impaired inside 12 months

rows.label: Assurance over an activity you ran 3 years ago
cells: Not automatically
No presumption, but the refrain rule has no end date: disclose, and the CAE decides

rows.label: Advisory work on an activity you used to run
cells: Yes
Disclose the possible impairment to the requesting party before accepting

rows.label: Assurance where the function earlier advised
cells: Yes, with conditions
The CAE confirms no impairment and assigns auditors so objectivity is managed

rows.label: Assurance over a function the CAE manages
cells: Only with outside oversight
An independent party outside the function oversees the engagement

subtopics.example: Last year Haruka, a senior internal auditor at a rail operator in Osaka, advised on the design of a ticket-refund process; Haruka never ran it. An assurance engagement on the process is now planned, so the rule for assurance after advice applies. The CAE confirms the advice did not impair objectivity and assigns Haruka to station cash counts, away from the design Haruka advised on.

review: Trace assurance engagements in previously advised areas to the documented objectivity confirmation
Compare advisory acceptances with disclosures made to the requesting party beforehand
evidence: Engagement planning files recording the impairment assessment and staffing decision
Written disclosures given to requesting parties before advisory work began
audit_focus.recommend: Record the objectivity assessment in the planning file before the function starts assurance work in an area it advised on.
audit_focus.decides: Staffing rests with the chief audit executive, not with the team

subtopics.isaca_rule: Ask: assurance or advisory, were you ever responsible for the activity, and how would it look? Must: no assurance over a responsibility held in the past 12 months; disclose before advisory work on one. Note 1B3.3 has a different 12-month rule.

exam_traps.trap: Disclosing a former responsibility lets the auditor go ahead with the assurance engagement.
exam_traps.why: Disclosure clears the advisory case only. For assurance inside 12 months objectivity is presumed impaired, so the auditor is kept off that work.

exam_traps.trap: An auditor may never do advisory work on an area they used to manage.
exam_traps.why: Advisory work there is permitted. The condition is disclosing the possible impairment to the requesting party before the engagement is accepted.

key_terms.definition: Advice, started by internal auditors or on request, with no assurance given and no management responsibility taken on.
The stakeholder who asks for an advisory service and agrees its nature and scope.

topics.overview: Once an impairment is recognized, something has to be done about it. This topic covers the policies that protect objectivity and the options for handling an impairment: telling the right party, moving the auditor, bringing in an outside party, and refusing gifts, rewards and favors.
can_do: Decide who must be told about an impairment, and when, for an internal auditor and for the chief audit executive
Weigh reassigning, rescheduling, rescoping and outsourcing against the facts of a scenario
Judge when an engagement needs an independent party outside the function to perform or oversee it
Determine whether a gift, favor or reward must be refused, and which policy to follow when two apply

subtopics.name: Disclosing an Impairment
subtopics.definition: Disclosure of an impairment is the prompt reporting of its details to the party who can act on it, whether it exists in fact or only in appearance.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Disclosure hands the decision to someone who is not affected. Working with an undeclared impairment is itself discreditable behavior.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 2.3 Disclosing Impairments to Objectivity): an internal auditor who learns of something that may impair their objectivity tells the chief audit executive (CAE) or a designated supervisor.
Must: if the work is affected, the CAE discusses it with the board, senior management, the management of the activity under review, or several, and determines the action.
Must: the CAE's own impairment, in fact or appearance, is disclosed to the board.
Must: when an impairment found after the engagement affects how reliable the results are, or seem, the CAE discusses it with those affected and determines the action.
May: a planning-stage concern about perception alone can be discussed by the CAE with the activity's management, senior management or both, explained and documented.

rows.label: An auditor's own impairment
cells: The internal auditor
The CAE or a designated supervisor

rows.label: An impairment affecting the work
cells: The CAE
One or more of: the board, senior management, the management of the activity under review

rows.label: The CAE's own impairment
cells: The CAE
The board

rows.label: Advisory work on a former responsibility
cells: The internal auditor
The party requesting the service, before accepting

subtopics.example: Three weeks into a payroll audit at a cocoa exporter in Abidjan, internal auditor Aya starts dating the payroll supervisor. No test result has changed, and Aya is tempted to wait until the engagement ends. Aya discloses the relationship to the CAE that week. The CAE discusses it with senior management and moves Aya to another engagement.

review: Compare disclosure dates with the dates auditors first knew of the impairment
Trace each disclosed impairment to a documented decision and its approver
evidence: Impairment disclosure register showing dates, recipients and resolutions
Board minutes showing receipt of a personal impairment disclosure
audit_focus.recommend: Define in the function's methodology who receives each kind of disclosure and how the decision is recorded.
audit_focus.decides: Staffing is the chief audit executive's decision; the board receives the chief audit executive's own disclosure

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: disclose promptly and upward. The auditor tells the CAE or a designated supervisor; the CAE determines the action; the CAE's own impairment goes to the board. May: a perception-only concern can be explained and documented.

exam_traps.trap: The auditor judges the impairment to be minor and carries on quietly.
exam_traps.why: The requirement is disclosure to the CAE or a designated supervisor. Whether it affects the work is for the CAE to determine, not the affected auditor.

exam_traps.trap: The CAE discloses a personal impairment to the chief executive officer.
exam_traps.why: The CAE's own impairment goes to the board. Reporting to a senior manager day to day does not replace that.

key_terms.definition: A supervisor designated to act for the chief audit executive, for example to receive impairment disclosures.
Reporting an impairment as soon as the auditor is aware of it.
Real, or reasonably seen as real by others; either triggers disclosure.

subtopics.name: Reassignment and Other Staffing Options
subtopics.definition: Reassignment is taking an impaired internal auditor off an engagement and giving the work to an unimpaired one; it is one of several options for managing an impairment.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Disclosure tells the right people; it does not remove the bias. The response has to match how serious the impairment is.
how_it_works: Must: the chief audit executive (CAE) sets methodologies for impairments, and auditors discuss impairments and act as those methodologies say.
May: for an impairment that cannot be avoided, the CAE may consider the options below. The Standards list them without ranking them.
Should: when planning resources, the CAE or a designated supervisor asks the auditors about current or potential impairments, including ones disclosed before.
Should: those who perform and those who supervise an engagement are both independent of the activity under review.
Fit the fix to the impairment's reach: reassign when a competent, unimpaired auditor is free; if the impairment touches only part of the work, handle that part (KaiSip's reading).

types.meaning: Take the impaired auditor off the engagement and assign another.
Move the engagement to a time when it can be properly staffed.
Have an outside provider perform or supervise the engagement.

subtopics.example: A bank in Muscat plans a treasury assurance engagement. Salim, the function's treasury specialist, discloses that a close relative was appointed head of the treasury desk last month. Layla, the CAE, has two other auditors with treasury experience. Layla reassigns the engagement to them, moves Salim to a branch audit, and records the disclosure and the decision.

review: Inspect planning records for the impairment discussion held before staffing
Compare the action chosen for each impairment with the documented methodology
evidence: Engagement staffing records showing reassignments and the reason for each
Internal audit plan changes showing rescheduled or rescoped engagements
audit_focus.recommend: Record, for every unavoidable impairment, the option the function chose and why the others did not fit.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive chooses how an impairment is managed, not the affected staff

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: follow the function's methodology for impairments. May: the CAE, not the impaired auditor, chooses among options the Standards list without ranking. Reassignment usually fits best when a competent, unimpaired auditor is available.

exam_traps.trap: The impaired auditor stays on because nobody else knows the area as well.
exam_traps.why: Expertise does not cancel bias. The function can get the knowledge another way: other staff, an expert borrowed from another department, or an outside provider.

exam_traps.trap: Once the impairment is disclosed, the engagement can go ahead unchanged.
exam_traps.why: Disclosure starts the process. If the impairment affects the work, the CAE still has to determine an action that manages it.

key_terms.definition: A measure that manages an actual, potential or perceived impairment to independence or objectivity, such as reassignment, outside oversight or outside assurance.
The chief audit executive's documented way of working, which internal auditors follow.
One that planning cannot remove, so it has to be disclosed and managed.

subtopics.name: Outside Parties to Perform or Oversee an Engagement
subtopics.definition: Outside performance or supervision means a party from beyond the internal audit function carries out an engagement, or oversees it, when nobody inside can do so objectively.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Some impairments reach the whole function: its head runs the area under review, or every available internal auditor used to work there. Reassignment cannot fix that. The full safeguards for such roles are in 1A8.4.
how_it_works: May: for an impairment that cannot be avoided, the chief audit executive (CAE) may have an outside provider perform or supervise the engagement (Standard 2.3).
It fits when no unimpaired, competent auditor or supervisor is available inside, as in a small function.
Must: an assurance engagement on another function the CAE runs is overseen by an independent party who is not part of internal audit (Standard 2.2).
Must: a long-term role outside audit goes in the charter; assurance over that area comes from elsewhere, such as an outside provider reporting to the board.
Must: during a temporary role and for 12 months after it, an independent third party gives that assurance, and the CAE plans the hand-back to management.

rows.label: Who it concerns
cells: Any internal auditor who was responsible for an activity
A CAE given a temporary role outside audit

rows.label: What the 12 months does
cells: Objectivity is presumed impaired for assurance over that activity
An independent third party gives the assurance over that area

rows.label: Which way it runs
cells: Back from the assurance work to when the responsibility was held
Forward from the day the temporary role ends

rows.label: What to do
cells: Stay off that work; another auditor performs it
Use the third party and plan the hand-back to management

subtopics.example: Ilze became the CAE of a vocational college in Riga five months ago, after running its admissions office; the only other internal auditor is a trainee. An admissions assurance engagement is due, and Ilze can neither perform nor supervise it. Ilze discloses the impairment to the board and contracts an outside firm to perform and supervise the engagement and report to the board.

review: Compare the charter with every role the chief audit executive holds outside audit
Trace assurance over those areas to a provider outside the function
evidence: Engagement letter of the outside provider and the reports it issued
Charter section listing the added roles and their safeguards
audit_focus.recommend: Propose to the board how each area the chief audit executive also manages will be independently assured.
audit_focus.decides: The board approves the added roles and acknowledges the impairment

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: when the impairment sits with the CAE, oversight, or the assurance itself, comes from an independent party outside the function. May: outsourcing is also an option for any impairment that cannot be avoided.

exam_traps.trap: A senior internal auditor can oversee assurance over an area the CAE manages.
exam_traps.why: Everyone in the function reports to the impaired person. Oversight must come from an independent party outside it.

exam_traps.trap: A small function with no unimpaired auditor has to cancel the engagement.
exam_traps.why: Having an outside provider perform or supervise the work is an option the CAE may consider. The impairment changes who does it.

key_terms.definition: Hiring a provider that is not part of the organization to carry out some or all internal audit work.
The board-approved document holding the function's mandate, position and reporting lines.

subtopics.name: Gifts, Rewards and Favors
subtopics.definition: A gift, reward or favor is anything of value, tangible or not, offered to an internal auditor; it must be refused when it may impair objectivity or be presumed to.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A gift creates a sense of obligation and, even when it does not, a reason for others to doubt the results. The test is how it looks, not what the auditor intends.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity): refuse any item, tangible or not, that may impair objectivity or be presumed to.
Intangible items count: hospitality, a job lead, a discount, event tickets or a personal favor.
Should: the function's methodologies set expectations on gifts, favors and rewards.
May: the chief audit executive may set a stricter gift policy than the organization's. Should: auditors follow it.
Must (Standard 1.2): the organization's gift rules bind auditors too; a looser audit manual never permits what the code bans.
Should: before accepting, ask whether it could look like influence or payment for favorable results.
subtopics.example: The organization-wide policy at a paper mill in Curitiba lets staff accept gifts worth up to 300 reais. The internal audit manual says auditors accept nothing from the management of an activity under review. After a warehouse audit, the logistics head sends Luana, the auditor, a hamper worth 150 reais. Luana follows the stricter manual, returns the hamper with thanks and logs it in the gift register.

review: Compare gift thresholds across both rulebooks and list each difference
Sample declared items against engagements the recipients worked on
evidence: Hospitality declarations filed by members of the function
Letters sent with returned items, showing dates
audit_focus.recommend: Publish one clear rulebook on gifts for the audit team and check declarations for exceptions.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive sets the function's gift rules through its methodology

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: refuse anything that may impair objectivity, or be presumed to, whatever its value. Should: where the organization's policy and the internal audit function's differ, follow the stricter one.

exam_traps.trap: The gift is under the organization's limit, so the auditor may keep it.
exam_traps.why: If the internal audit function's policy is stricter, the auditor should follow that one. A permitted value does not settle how the gift looks.

exam_traps.trap: Only cash or expensive items can impair objectivity.
exam_traps.why: The rule covers tangible and intangible items of any size, favors and rewards included. What matters is whether objectivity may be, or be presumed, impaired.

key_terms.definition: Something of value you cannot hold, such as a favor, an introduction, hospitality or a discount.
Reasonably assumed by others to affect judgment, whether or not it does.
The written collection of the function's methodologies that tells internal auditors how to work.

topics.overview: Competency is what an auditor knows and can do. This topic covers the rule that auditors must have, or obtain, the competencies the work needs; the professional skills the syllabus lists (communication, relationship building, critical thinking, persuasion, research, curiosity and handling change); and the signs that more professional development is needed.
can_do: Apply the have-or-obtain rule when an engagement needs a skill the team lacks
Shape a message so it is accurate, clear, concise and useful to the person receiving it
Use evidence and respectful discussion to settle a disagreement with management or a teammate
Recognize the signs that an internal auditor needs further professional development

subtopics.name: Competency: Have It or Obtain It
subtopics.definition: Competency is the knowledge, skills and abilities an internal auditor needs; auditors must hold them, or get them, for the work they take on.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Work done without the right competencies gives conclusions nobody should rely on. But a skills gap is a reason to find the skill, not refuse.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 3.1 Competency): have or obtain the competencies your work needs, knowledge of the Standards included, and take on only work you are, or can become, competent for.
Must: the chief audit executive (CAE) ensures the function as a whole has the competencies for the services in its charter, or obtains them.
May: fill a gap by training, a guest auditor, other assurance providers or an outside firm (Standard 10.2); a borrowed expert must not be responsible for the area audited.
Must: raise inappropriate or insufficient engagement resources with the CAE (Standard 13.5).

The Internal Auditing Competency Framework, a practice guide and not a requirement, groups competencies as internal auditing, professional, governance and risk management, and operational area, at four proficiency levels.
subtopics.example: A Bangkok logistics firm's plan includes an assurance engagement on warehouse robotics, a subject no internal auditor knows. Anong, the engagement supervisor, could cancel it or staff it and hope. Instead Anong raises the gap with the CAE, who brings in an automation engineer as a supervised guest auditor.

review: Compare skills each planned engagement needs with the assigned team's documented competencies
Trace each identified skills gap to training, hiring or an outside provider
evidence: Competency assessment of the function against the internal audit plan
Contracts and qualifications of external providers and guest auditors
audit_focus.recommend: Keep a current skills inventory for the audit team and a documented plan to close each gap it shows.
audit_focus.decides: The board approves the budget that funds training and outside expertise

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: take on only work you are, or can become, competent for, and raise a resource gap with the CAE. May: fill the gap by training, a guest auditor or an outside provider.

exam_traps.trap: The team lacks the skill, so the engagement must be declined.
exam_traps.why: The competency can be obtained through training, a guest auditor, another assurance provider or an external service provider.

exam_traps.trap: An experienced auditor can pick up an unfamiliar technical area alone during fieldwork.
exam_traps.why: Accepting work with no competency and no plan to attain it breaks Standard 3.1. Learning on an engagement is fine under proper supervision.

key_terms.definition: An expert from elsewhere in the organization who joins an engagement to supply a missing skill.
An outside firm or specialist engaged to supply skills, tools or staff for internal audit work.
How far a person has advanced in a skill or subject: basic, intermediate, advanced or expert.

subtopics.memory_aid: Have the competency or obtain it.

subtopics.name: Communicating Clearly and Building Trust
subtopics.definition: Communication skills are an internal auditor's ability to give the right person an accurate, clear message, in writing or speech; relationship building earns the trust that makes people listen.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A correct finding changes nothing if the reader cannot follow it or does not trust its author.
how_it_works: Must: the chief audit executive (CAE) sets methodologies so communications are accurate, complete, objective, clear, concise, constructive and timely (Standard 11.2).
Should: fit the message to the reader (the board needs different detail from the area's managers), use the organization's plain words and define any unavoidable technical term.
Must: communicate effectively all through the engagement (Standard 13.1). Should: mix formal, informal, written and spoken methods.
Must: the CAE sets an approach for building relationships and trust with key stakeholders, with formal and informal communication (Standard 11.1).
Should: meet operational managers and staff regularly; steady informal contact builds trust and candor. Rotation may protect objectivity.
Should (Standard 11.3, a consideration): acknowledge satisfactory performance in engagement communications, especially a practice other units could adopt.
subtopics.example: Nadia, an internal auditor at a university in Cairo, drafts a finding: 'Dual-auth exception, ctrl RF-02, above DoA limit'. The supervisor asks who will read it. For the audit committee Nadia rewrites it: 'Refunds above the limit were paid without a second approval.' Same facts; now the reader can act on them.

review: Sample final communications against the function's style guide and quality criteria
Compare the issue dates of communications with the end of fieldwork
evidence: Stakeholder survey results on the quality of internal audit communications
Supervisory review notes on drafts of engagement communications
Calendar of regular meetings between auditors and operational managers
audit_focus.recommend: Adopt a style guide and have supervisors on the audit team test each draft against the seven qualities.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive approves each final communication and who receives it; management acts on it

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: communicate effectively throughout the engagement, following the function's methodologies. Should: fit the message to the reader, use plain words and keep up regular informal contact. A message the reader cannot use has not been communicated.

exam_traps.trap: A technically precise finding is clear enough; understanding it is the reader's job.
exam_traps.why: Clear means easily understood by the intended reader. Auditors should avoid needless technical language and define terms the reader may not know.

exam_traps.trap: Keeping your distance from the people you audit is the only way to protect objectivity.
exam_traps.why: The Standards expect relationships and trust with stakeholders, built through regular formal and informal contact. Rotation protects objectivity; avoiding people does not.

key_terms.definition: The communication issued at the end of an engagement with its results, often a written report.
Worded to help the reader improve, in a cooperative tone, not to blame.
The function's written rules for how its communications are worded and laid out.

subtopics.name: Critical Thinking, Persuasion and Disagreement
subtopics.definition: Critical thinking is reasoning from evidence to a sound judgment; persuasion and negotiation are the skills of bringing others to accept that judgment, or settling fairly where they do not.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Hard problems rarely have one obvious fix, and a right answer nobody accepts changes nothing.
how_it_works: Critical thinking: use knowledge, experience and logic to judge a risk's significance, with management's input, and trace findings to root causes.
Management decides the action; internal auditors may offer options. Should: weigh each for feasibility, cost against benefit and bringing the risk within tolerance, and agree one that does.
Must: if management disagrees with the results, discuss and seek a mutual understanding; failing that, you need not change the results without a valid reason (Standard 13.1).
Must: follow the methodology that lets both sides state their positions. Should: the chief audit executive (CAE) works with senior management to resolve what remains.
Should (Standard 12.3): the CAE sets a way to settle audit-team judgment differences, such as further inquiry and recording each view in the workpapers, not deference to rank.
subtopics.example: At a Leeds building society's closing meeting, the lending manager rejects a finding on loan file reviews. Internal auditor Callum walks through three sample files and listens to the manager's point about a system change. One detail was wrong, a valid reason, so Callum corrects it. The finding stands, and both positions are recorded.

review: Sample workpapers for root cause analysis that goes beyond the visible symptom
Trace disputed findings to the record of each side's position
evidence: Final communications that carry management's differing view
Workpapers documenting differing views inside the audit team
audit_focus.recommend: Coach internal audit staff to present several options where no single fix is obvious, and to record disagreements.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides its response; the chief audit executive approves the final wording

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: discuss a disagreement, seek mutual understanding and follow the methodology for stating both positions. Without a valid reason you need not change the results, and you never soften them to please someone. Should: the CAE helps resolve what remains.

exam_traps.trap: Good persuasion means holding your position until management gives in.
exam_traps.why: The aim is a shared, evidence-based understanding. An auditor who will not listen misses valid reasons to correct the results.

exam_traps.trap: Rewording a finding to satisfy an unhappy manager is good relationship building.
exam_traps.why: Relationships rest on trust and candor. Softening a finding to please someone breaks the honesty rule.

key_terms.definition: The deeper reason a gap exists, as opposed to its visible symptom.
Both sides see the facts and their meaning the same way, even if they differ on what to do.
Working through differing positions to an outcome both sides can accept, without giving up the facts.

subtopics.name: Research, Curiosity, Change and Continuing Development
subtopics.definition: Continuing professional development is the ongoing learning by which internal auditors keep and grow their competencies; research, curiosity and readiness for change are habits that drive it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Knowledge goes out of date, fastest in technology. An auditor who stops learning slowly loses the competency the Standards require.
how_it_works: Research: draw on several sources (earlier engagements, laws, guidance, interviews, data). Should (Standard 13.4): research recommended practice and compare management's criteria with other organizations'.
Curiosity: skepticism requires an inquisitive attitude, and the chief audit executive (CAE) should encourage auditors' curiosity.
Change: the internal audit plan must be dynamic and a changed work program must be approved promptly; training may introduce new technology or changed practices.
Must (Standard 3.2): every internal auditor, the CAE included, keeps developing their competencies through education and training; certified auditors also meet their certification's rules.
Each auditor owns their development. Must: the CAE evaluates competencies and helps through training, feedback or mentoring. Should: every auditor gets regular ethics training.
Signs of a need: new subjects or technology, a changed law or standard, feedback showing a skill gap, a new role, or stale knowledge in fast-changing areas.
subtopics.example: Annika, a senior internal auditor at a Zurich seed company, earned a certification six years ago and has since audited only procurement. A supervisor's review finds Annika's access testing on a new cloud platform used outdated methods; part is redone. Annika books cloud security training and asks to shadow a specialist on the next engagement.

review: Compare completed learning hours with each certifying body's stated minimum
Inspect performance reviews for competency gaps that led to no action
evidence: Continuing education records obtained from the certifying body or training provider
Individual development plans agreed with supervisors
Approved budget showing the amount set aside for learning
audit_focus.recommend: Set minimum learning expectations for audit staff and include the cost in the budget request to the board.
audit_focus.decides: The board approves the internal audit budget, including training funds

subtopics.isaca_rule: Certification is a starting point. Must: keep developing your competencies and meet your certification's continuing education rules. Should: learn about trends and emerging risks. A gap shown by feedback or change means act now.

exam_traps.trap: Once certified, further training is a personal choice.
exam_traps.why: Continuing development is required of every internal auditor, and certified auditors must also meet their certification's rules.

exam_traps.trap: Following last year's work program exactly shows discipline and consistency.
exam_traps.why: A work program rests on current planning information. When the activity has changed, old steps test controls that may no longer exist.

key_terms.definition: Structured learning a certifying body requires in a set period to keep a credential.
The approved list of steps an engagement will perform to meet its objectives.
A new or changing risk that is not yet well understood.

topics.overview: Due professional care is the standard of diligence expected of a prudent, competent internal auditor. This topic covers what care requires and does not require, the factors an auditor weighs in applying it, and professional skepticism: the questioning attitude toward whether information can be relied on.
can_do: Explain why due professional care does not mean testing everything or never missing anything
Pick out, in a planning scenario, the factors that care asks the internal auditor to weigh
Apply professional skepticism to an unsupported statement without assuming dishonesty

subtopics.name: What Due Professional Care Means
subtopics.definition: Due professional care is the level of attention, judgment and healthy doubt a sensible, capable internal auditor would apply when planning and carrying out the work.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Care sets a realistic bar. It protects those who rely on the work from sloppiness, and it protects the auditor from an impossible promise of perfection.
how_it_works: Must (Principle 4 Exercise Due Professional Care): plan and perform the work with the judgment, diligence and skepticism of a prudent, competent internal auditor.
Care has three parts: following the Standards, weighing the nature and circumstances of the work, and applying professional skepticism.
Auditors act in the best interests of those receiving the service, but are not expected to be infallible (never wrong).
So care is judged by the quality of the planning and the work, not by whether every error was found.
Conformance (following the Standards and the function's methodologies) is part of care. If a requirement cannot be met, the chief audit executive must document and communicate why.
subtopics.example: Sanne, an internal auditor at a Dutch pension fund, tests a risk-based sample of benefit payments, follows up every exception and has the work reviewed. A year later a fraud surfaces in a payment type the risk assessment rated low. A quality review confirms Sanne planned, tested and documented as a prudent auditor would. Care was exercised. Sanne helps update the risk assessment.

review: Sample engagements against the Standards and the function's documented methodologies
Inspect workpapers for evidence of timely supervisory review
evidence: Quality assessment results on how far engagements conformed
Workpapers with dated supervisor sign-offs
audit_focus.recommend: Verify through supervision and quality reviews that the audit team's engagements follow the Standards and the methodologies.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive determines how nonconformance is documented and communicated

subtopics.isaca_rule: Due professional care is reasonable care, not a guarantee. Must: plan and work as a prudent, competent auditor would, following the Standards. The test is the quality of the work, not whether every error was found.

exam_traps.trap: An auditor who exercises due care will find every significant problem.
exam_traps.why: Auditors are not expected to be infallible. Care is judged by the quality of the planning and the work, not by a perfect outcome.

exam_traps.trap: Care means examining every transaction to be safe.
exam_traps.why: Care weighs cost against benefit and the significance of risks. Testing everything where risk is low takes resources from higher risks.

key_terms.definition: A careful, sensible professional whose likely conduct is the yardstick for due professional care.
Meeting the requirements of the Global Internal Audit Standards.
A requirement of the Standards that was not met; it is documented and disclosed as the Standards direct.

subtopics.name: The Factors Care Weighs
subtopics.definition: The due professional care factors are what Standard 4.2 requires internal auditors to assess about a service: its nature, circumstances and requirements.
subtopics.why_it_matters: These factors decide how much work is enough and where to aim it, tying each engagement to the organization's goals and risks.
how_it_works: Strategy and objectives: what the organization and the activity under review aim to achieve, and whether the two line up.
Interests: those of the people served and of other stakeholders, the public included.
Governance, risk management, and control processes: how adequate and effective they are, weighed for the plan and again for the activity in each engagement.
Cost against benefit: the resources the work uses against the value it is likely to bring.
Risk: how complex, material or significant the risks are to the activity under review (not only the organization), and how probable significant errors, fraud and noncompliance are.
The work itself: how much, how quickly, and which techniques and tools fit. Should: weigh a full-population test, which software makes practical, against a sample (Standard 14.1).
subtopics.example: Planning a procurement engagement at a Mexican car parts maker, internal auditor Luis finds the vendor approval control's design cannot work: one clerk both creates and approves vendors. Testing its operation all year would take three weeks and prove little. Luis reports the design gap as a finding and moves those hours to payments, where fraud risk is higher.

review: Inspect planning notes for the organization's and the activity's objectives
Compare budgeted hours per area with the engagement risk assessment's ranking
evidence: Engagement risk assessment covering errors, fraud and noncompliance
Planning notes on the expected costs and benefits of the work
Budget-to-actual hours with reasons for variances
audit_focus.recommend: Require planning notes from the audit team that show how risk and cost shaped the extent of testing.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive or a delegated engagement supervisor approves the work program

subtopics.isaca_rule: Care is proportion. Must: weigh every Standard 4.2 factor, cost against benefit and the probability of fraud included. Effort follows the objectives, the risks and the likely value; fully testing a control whose design already fails is rarely worth the cost.

exam_traps.trap: Cost should never limit audit work; more testing is always the careful choice.
exam_traps.why: Weighing the work's cost against its likely benefit is a required factor. Effort without added value takes resources from higher risks.

exam_traps.trap: Fraud is considered only when the engagement is a fraud investigation.
exam_traps.why: How probable significant errors, fraud and noncompliance are is a factor of due professional care in every internal audit service.

key_terms.definition: Comparing what a piece of audit work will cost with the value it is likely to produce.
How large or important something is, relative to its context.
Failure to follow a law, regulation, contract, policy or other requirement.

subtopics.memory_aid: Care is proportion: effort follows objectives, risk and value.

subtopics.name: Professional Skepticism
subtopics.definition: Professional skepticism is an unbiased, questioning attitude toward information: the internal auditor tests whether it can be relied on instead of taking it on trust.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Conclusions built on unverified statements can be wrong however carefully they are written. Skepticism keeps judgments resting on facts and logic, not on trust.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 4.3 Professional Skepticism): apply it when planning and when performing internal audit services.
Must: stay inquisitive. Curiosity and a willingness to look below the surface are part of the attitude.
Must: critically assess each item's reliability. Information obtained directly by the auditor or from an independent source, or corroborated, is more reliable (Standard 14.1).
Must: be straightforward and honest when raising a concern or asking about an inconsistency.
Must: seek more evidence when information could be false, misleading, incomplete or inconsistent. Evidence that is reliable, sufficient and consistent does not call for more.
Skepticism is unbiased: it doubts claims, not people's honesty.
subtopics.example: During an inventory audit at a furniture maker in Vilnius, the warehouse manager tells Rasa, the internal auditor, that the finance director approved all stock write-offs, though the approval emails were lost in a system migration. Rasa thanks the manager, then asks the finance director directly, checks the migration logs and compares write-off patterns with earlier years. Two write-offs turn out to have no approval.

review: Sample workpapers for management statements accepted without corroborating evidence
Trace inconsistent information noted in workpapers to its follow-up
evidence: Workpapers showing how the auditor validated information received
Supervisor review notes asking for further support
Records showing misleading information treated as a finding
audit_focus.recommend: Train internal audit staff to corroborate what management tells them and to document how each statement was validated.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive or a delegated engagement supervisor judges whether evidence supports the conclusion

subtopics.isaca_rule: Trust is not evidence. Must: critically assess what you are told, be straightforward when asking about an inconsistency, and seek more evidence. Sound practice, not a Standards line: once facts suggest deliberate concealment, stop asking the person concerned and report (see 1D3.3).

exam_traps.trap: Skepticism means assuming that management is hiding something.
exam_traps.why: Skepticism questions the information, not the person's character. The auditor doubts a claim until evidence supports it and stays unbiased.

exam_traps.trap: A senior manager's clear statement is enough support for a conclusion.
exam_traps.why: Statements are validated with evidence, not accepted because of rank.

key_terms.definition: The auditor's own record of the planning, tests and evidence behind an engagement's results.
To confirm one piece of information with another from a different source.
How far information can be trusted, given its source and whether other evidence agrees with it.
Facts or statements that do not agree with each other and so need follow-up.

topics.topic_name: Confidentiality and proper use of information
topics.overview: Internal auditors see information that few others in the organization can. This topic covers why that access brings a duty, how information may and may not be used, how it is protected through its life, and the narrow cases where confidential information is disclosed.
can_do: Apply the organization's policies, the law and the function's methodologies when handling engagement information
Recognize misuse of information, including use for personal gain that seems to harm nobody
Choose a fitting protection for sensitive information at each stage, from first access to disposal
Decide whether a request to release confidential information rests on a legal or professional duty, and who authorizes it

subtopics.name: Access to Information and the Duty of Confidentiality
subtopics.definition: Confidentiality is the internal auditor's duty to use the information they receive only for professional purposes and to keep it from anyone not authorized to have it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The mandate gives internal auditors unrestricted access to records, people and systems. People cooperate only if they trust that what auditors learn will be handled properly.
how_it_works: Principle 5 Maintain Confidentiality: auditors use and protect information appropriately.
The information is often confidential, proprietary or personally identifiable, such as salaries and personnel records.
The duty covers paper and digital records and also what is said aloud, in formal meetings or casual talk.
Ownership: access is not ownership. The information stays the organization's, or another party's, and the auditor uses it only for professional purposes.
Must: follow the laws, regulations and policies on privacy when handling personal data. Should: the chief audit executive periodically confirms what access auditors still need.
Unauthorized disclosure is barred inside the organization as well as outside it.
subtopics.example: Internal auditor Siddharth at an Indian software company is testing payroll controls and sees the salaries of the whole leadership team. At lunch a colleague from marketing asks what the new sales head earns. The colleague is an employee but has no authorization to know. Siddharth declines, mentions nothing from the engagement, and keeps the payroll extract inside the restricted engagement folder.

review: Compare who can open engagement folders with the assigned engagement teams
Inspect signed confidentiality acknowledgments for every auditor and guest auditor
evidence: System access listings for engagement files holding personal data
Signed confidentiality or nondisclosure agreements
audit_focus.recommend: Confirm periodically that each member of the audit team still needs the access to information they hold.
audit_focus.decides: Information owners grant access; the chief audit executive reviews whether it is still required

subtopics.isaca_rule: Access is for the work, and for nothing else. Must: use information only for professional purposes and share it only with people authorized to receive it. A fellow employee is not authorized just by being an employee.

exam_traps.trap: Confidentiality is about outsiders; anything can be shared with colleagues.
exam_traps.why: Information is protected from unauthorized access and disclosure internally as well as externally. Authorization, not employment, decides who may see it.

exam_traps.trap: Only written records are confidential; a conversation is not.
exam_traps.why: The duty also covers information that comes from spoken communication, informal discussions included.

key_terms.definition: Data that can be linked to a specific person, such as a name with a salary or health record.
Information an organization owns and keeps private because it has commercial value.
Freedom to reach the data, records, people and property the work needs.
Anyone, inside or outside the organization, without permission to receive the information.

subtopics.name: Using Information Properly
subtopics.definition: Proper use of information means an internal auditor handles it as policies, procedures, laws and regulations require, and never for personal gain or against the organization's legitimate interests.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Misuse can bring fines, reputational harm and personal liability, and it ends the trust that unrestricted access depends on. The harm does not have to be visible to be real.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 5.1 Use of Information): whenever you use information, the applicable laws, regulations, policies and procedures govern how.
Must not: use it for personal gain, whether or not anyone appears to lose.
Must not: use it against the organization's legitimate, ethical aims.
The rules cover the whole life of information: access, collection, transfer, storage and destruction.
Should: also know and follow any policies and procedures covering third-party information you can reach, such as a supplier's data.
Should: the chief audit executive explains the expectations. May: auditors are asked for a signed acknowledgment.
subtopics.example: While auditing a planned acquisition at a listed mining company in Perth, internal auditor Kirra learns the target's name before any announcement. Kirra's cousin trades shares and asks for tips. Nobody would ever know. Kirra refuses, buys no shares, and keeps the file in the restricted workspace as the insider information policy requires.

review: Compare auditors' personal trading declarations with engagements involving price-sensitive information
Inspect how engagement data extracts were transferred, stored and destroyed
evidence: Data transfer and deletion logs for engagement extracts
Insider list entries for internal audit staff
audit_focus.recommend: Brief the audit team on the information-use rules and keep each member's signed acknowledgment.
audit_focus.decides: The organization sets its information policies; the chief audit executive sets the function's

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: use engagement information only as law and policy allow, never for personal gain and never against the organization's legitimate aims, even when nobody is hurt or finds out. Should: follow the policies covering third-party data too.

exam_traps.trap: Using engagement information privately is fine as long as the organization suffers no loss.
exam_traps.why: The bar on personal gain does not depend on harm. Trading on, selling or passing on inside knowledge is the Standards' own example of misuse.

exam_traps.trap: The audit mandate overrides privacy and data protection rules.
exam_traps.why: Unrestricted access lets auditors obtain information. How they use and handle it is still governed by policies, procedures, laws and regulations.

key_terms.definition: Any benefit to the auditor or people close to them, in money or otherwise.
Financial, strategic or operational knowledge, not yet public, that could move a share price or help a competitor.
The stages information passes through, from first access to final destruction.
Data belonging to an outside party, such as a supplier or customer, that the auditor can reach.

subtopics.name: Protecting Information and Engagement Records
subtopics.definition: Protection of information is the set of steps an internal auditor takes so that information gathered in the work is not seen, copied, lost or released without authorization.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Most leaks are accidents: a misdirected email, a lost laptop, an old extract nobody deleted. Auditors must manage that risk, not just mean well.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 5.2 Protection of Information): know your protection duties and follow the laws, policies and procedures on confidentiality, privacy and information security.
The function's methodologies cover custody, retention and disposal of engagement records, and their release to internal and external parties.
They also cover confidential information, access rights and copies once these are no longer needed.
Must: manage the risk of exposing information by accident.
Usual protections: encryption (scrambling data so only a key holder can read it), passwords, controlled email distribution and restricted physical access.
Must: the chief audit executive (CAE) ensures that people assisting the function, such as guest auditors and outside providers, follow the same rules.
subtopics.example: A data specialist on contract helped the internal audit function of a public library service in Cardiff test membership records. Months later an access review finds that the specialist still holds a copy of the membership extract on a personal drive. Rhys, the CAE, has the copy deleted and confirmed in writing, removes the specialist's remaining access, and adds a data-return sign-off to every contractor assignment.

review: Compare auditors' current system access with engagements that have closed
Sample closed engagements for raw data extracts kept beyond the retention rule
evidence: Access removal records dated against engagement closure dates
Encryption status reports for internal audit laptops and shared drives
Disposal logs matched to the record-keeping schedule
audit_focus.recommend: Set retention, disposal and access removal steps in the methodology and monitor that the audit team follows them.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive sets the function's record-handling methodology

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: protect information through its whole life and manage the risk of accidental exposure; the CAE must hold helpers to the same rules. Should: once the need ends, remove access and handle copies as the methodology says.

exam_traps.trap: Keeping every data extract forever is the safest way to support the findings.
exam_traps.why: Engagement documentation is retained as law and policy require. Copies and access no longer needed add exposure and are handled as the methodology says.

exam_traps.trap: Protection rules bind the function's employees, not a contractor helping on one engagement.
exam_traps.why: The CAE must ensure that individuals assisting the internal audit function follow the same protection requirements.

key_terms.definition: The workpapers and other documents created or collected during an engagement.
Who holds a record and is responsible for keeping it safe.
How long a record is kept before it is disposed of, as law and policy set.

subtopics.name: When Confidential Information Is Disclosed
subtopics.definition: Authorized disclosure is the release of confidential information to a party entitled to it, or under a legal or professional responsibility, by the route that law, policy and methodology set.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Confidentiality is not secrecy at any price. It never justifies hiding a finding from the board, and it gives way when the law requires disclosure.
how_it_works: Must not (Standard 5.2): give confidential information to an unauthorized party, unless a legal or professional responsibility calls for it.
Reporting results to the board and senior management is authorized. A finding is never left out on confidentiality grounds (Standard 1.1).
Must: report legal violations to those with authority to act, and make the disclosures the law requires (Standard 1.3).
Must: before a final communication leaves the organization, the chief audit executive (CAE) seeks whatever advice is required from legal counsel, senior management or both (Standard 11.3).
Should: the CAE consults legal counsel on legal requirements and on protections such as legal privilege.

rows.label: The board asks for the full engagement results
cells: Yes
Normal reporting; nothing is held back as confidential

rows.label: A manager from another unit asks for workpapers
cells: Not without authorization
The release rules in the function's methodology

rows.label: A law or regulation requires the disclosure
cells: Yes
As the law requires, with legal counsel's advice where needed

rows.label: A friend or a journalist asks
cells: No
No authorization and no legal or professional duty

subtopics.example: The external auditor of an airline in Port Louis emails Anjali, an internal auditor, asking for the full workpapers of a fuel hedging engagement by Friday. Anjali knows the audit partner well, but sends nothing. Anjali passes the request to the CAE, who follows the function's release methodology and takes advice from legal counsel before deciding what is shared.

review: Trace each external release of engagement records to its documented authorization
Compare distribution lists of final communications with the approved recipients
evidence: Log of legally required releases and of releases cleared by legal counsel
Documented restrictions on distributing workpapers and final communications
Requests for records, with the decision and its approver
audit_focus.recommend: Name in the function's methodology who may approve each kind of release of engagement records.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive decides who receives final engagement communications

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: disclose confidential information only to an authorized party or under a legal or professional duty, by the set route; the CAE seeks required advice before an outside release. Confidentiality never keeps a finding from the board.

exam_traps.trap: The matter is confidential, so the auditor leaves it out of the report to the board.
exam_traps.why: The board is an authorized recipient of results. Leaving out a finding breaks the honesty requirement; sensitivity is managed by restricting distribution.

exam_traps.trap: Confidentiality lets an auditor refuse a disclosure that the law requires.
exam_traps.why: The duty has an explicit exception for legal or professional responsibility, and auditors must make the disclosures that laws and regulations require.

key_terms.definition: A duty set by law, regulation or professional standards that requires a disclosure.
Legal protection that can keep certain communications with lawyers from being disclosed.
The function's rules for who may receive engagement records and who authorizes it.

key_terminologies.Domain II: The second domain of the Global Internal Audit Standards, on ethics and professionalism: Principles 1 to 5 and Standards 1.1 to 5.2.
key_terminologies.Consideration for Implementation: A 'should' or 'may' in a standard: preferred or optional practice, not mandatory.
key_terminologies.Chief audit executive (CAE): The head of the internal audit function, whatever the job title.
key_terminologies.Engagement: One piece of internal audit work with its own objectives and scope.
key_terminologies.Engagement supervisor: The internal auditor who supervises an engagement: the chief audit executive, or a delegate for whom the chief audit executive stays accountable.
key_terminologies.Board: The highest governing body, such as the directors or audit committee; where several govern, the body (or bodies) empowered to give internal audit its mandate.
key_terminologies.Senior management: The top executives, usually including the chief executive officer, who answer to the board.
key_terminologies.Assurance services: Engagements where internal auditors test an activity against criteria and state a conclusion others can rely on.
key_terminologies.Advisory services: Advice, started by internal auditors or on request, with no assurance given and no management responsibility taken on.
key_terminologies.Integrity: Honesty plus the courage to act on the facts, whatever the pressure; the base of the other four ethics principles.
key_terminologies.Professional courage: Communicating truthfully and acting properly in a dilemma or under pressure.
key_terminologies.Discreditable behavior: Conduct that harms trust in the internal auditor, the organization or the profession, such as lying about a credential.
key_terminologies.Objectivity: Each internal auditor's unbiased state of mind when judging evidence.
key_terminologies.Independence: The function's freedom, gained from its position, to do and report its work without being steered by those it audits.
key_terminologies.Impairment to objectivity: A situation, activity or relationship that may bias an auditor's judgment, in fact or in appearance.
key_terminologies.Self-review bias: Losing a critical eye when assessing work one designed, decided or performed oneself.
key_terminologies.Familiarity bias: Letting assumptions from past experience stand in for fresh evidence, which weakens professional skepticism.
key_terminologies.Conflict of interest: A competing personal or professional interest that could sway an auditor's judgment or seem to.
key_terminologies.Perceived impairment: Something that looks like an impairment of independence or objectivity even when none exists.
key_terminologies.Refrain rule: An internal auditor must not assess a specific activity they were previously responsible for; the Standards set no end date.
key_terminologies.12-month presumption: For assurance, objectivity is presumed impaired when the internal auditor was responsible for the activity in the previous 12 months.
key_terminologies.Safeguard: A measure that manages an actual, potential or perceived impairment to independence or objectivity, such as reassignment, outside oversight or outside assurance.
key_terminologies.Designated supervisor: A supervisor designated to act for the chief audit executive, for example to receive impairment disclosures.
key_terminologies.Competency: What an auditor knows and can do, at the level the job needs.
key_terminologies.Continuing professional development: Ongoing education, training and experience that keep an auditor's competencies current.
key_terminologies.Due professional care: The diligence, judgment and skepticism of a prudent, competent internal auditor; reasonable care, not perfection.
key_terminologies.Professional skepticism: An unbiased, questioning attitude: critically assessing whether information is reliable before relying on it.
key_terminologies.Confidentiality: Keeping information gained at work for work purposes alone, and away from anyone not authorized to have it.
key_terminologies.Methodologies: The chief audit executive's documented way of working, which internal auditors follow.
